questions.q: What connectivity property makes the surface code especially well-matched to real quantum hardware?
options: Every stabilizer only touches 4 physically neighboring qubits on a 2D grid, matching real nearest-neighbor qubit wiring
It requires every qubit to be connected to every other qubit on the chip
It requires no physical qubits to be connected to each other at all
It only works on hardware with exactly 7 qubits
questions.explain: The surface code's stabilizers are local (touching only 4 neighboring qubits), which matches how real superconducting and other platforms are physically wired -- unlike codes needing long-range connectivity.

questions.q: Why does a code's error threshold matter in practice, not just its minimum distance?
options: A code needs a threshold that real, achievable physical error rates can realistically fall below, or increasing its distance won't actually help
Minimum distance and threshold are the same quantity under different names
Threshold only matters for classical codes, never for quantum codes
A lower threshold is always better than a higher one
questions.explain: Per the threshold theorem (developed in chapter 6), below the threshold, scaling up distance helps exponentially; above it, scaling up doesn't help -- so a favorable, achievable threshold matters as much as raw distance.

questions.q: Using the verified table, how many total physical qubits does a distance-9 surface code need to protect 1 logical qubit?
questions.explain: The verified formula total = 2d^2-1 gives 2(81)-1 = 161 for d=9, matching the table in the lesson.

questions.q: Why does the surface code need dramatically more physical qubits than the Steane code for comparable protection?
options: The surface code's distance is a tunable knob that can be increased for more protection, unlike the Steane code's fixed distance of 3, so higher protection directly costs more qubits
The surface code is strictly worse than the Steane code in every respect
The Steane code actually requires more qubits than the surface code at every distance
The surface code cannot correct any errors at distance 3
questions.explain: The Steane code is fixed at distance 3 (7 qubits), while the surface code can be built at any distance d, trading more physical qubits for exponentially better protection -- a tradeoff chapter 6 develops fully.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by calling the surface code the 'leading candidate' rather than a 'solved' approach?
options: It is the architecture most real hardware roadmaps are building toward, but running it at the distances needed for useful fault-tolerant computation remains a forward-looking engineering goal, not achieved today
It means the surface code has already been fully implemented at useful scale on real hardware
It means no other code has ever been seriously considered for hardware
It means the surface code requires no further research or engineering
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that 'leading candidate' describes the current favored research and engineering direction, not a claim that useful-scale fault-tolerant computation has already been achieved.
